Debate: Is the Flat Tax a Libertarian Reform?

Outside of taxes not being overly burdensome because of their effect on liberty, I don't think libertarianism really pushes any particular type of tax. We can argue what level of taxes receipts are necessary and the best to get that with minimal negative externalities, but something like a flat tax on income or a progressive tax on income or a consumption tax or a property tax is not inherently libertarian. The devil will always be in the details.

No taxes is a libertarian reform. Anything else is just a step in the right direction.

Further reading: https://mises.org/library/flat-tax-not-flat-and-fairtax-not-fair
Are steps in the right direction reform?

And that is why the radical libertarian is not only an abolitionist, but also refuses to think in such terms as a Four Year Plan for some sort of stately and measured procedure for reducing the State. The radical — whether he be anarchist or laissez-faire — cannot think in such terms as, e.g., "Well, the first year, we'll cut the income tax by 2 percent, abolish the ICC, and cut the minimum wage; the second year we'll abolish the minimum wage, cut the income tax by another 2 percent, and reduce welfare payments by 3 percent, etc." The radical cannot think in such terms, because the radical regards the State as our mortal enemy, which must be hacked away at wherever and whenever we can. To the radical libertarian, we must take any and every opportunity to chop away at the State, whether it's to reduce or abolish a tax, a budget appropriation, or a regulatory power. And the radical libertarian is insatiable in this appetite until the State has been abolished, or — for minarchists — dwindled down to a tiny, laissez-faire role.

A young woman. A good neighborhood. A gentle, quiet jog. A car. Grey, maybe black. Too dark to tell. It's driving down the road, maybe it's following her. Maybe not. The woman doesn't know and doesn't care. She's jogging home, earbuds in her ears. The car is behind her. She notices it, but ignores it. She turns a corner. So does the car. She is well trained by her father, who was ex-SWAT. Died on the job, when she was 14. She was raised by her mother, but not before her dad taught her how to pay attention and infer details. There's a grey car on a dark road at 22:00 following a young, good-looking woman. You can figure out what's happening here.

The woman picks up her pace and turns to another street. Now she's taking the shortcut home. Or should she? It's much faster, but it goes through alleyways. Dark places, darker than the street. It's worth it, the car can't fit down those alleys. She picks up the pace again, and jogs towards the first of three alleys, separated by streets. The car speeds up a little. She goes faster. The car slows back down, then stomps on the gas, quickly accelerating towards her. She stops abruptly, just before being in the street. The car passes and then stops. She sprints to the alley and runs down it, never looking behind her. As she's running she has... a vision. A white man, dark hair, good looking. He's wearing a grey dress shirt. It looks different from a normal dress shirt, almost like the material is more durable. He's wearing tactical pants with kneepads in them. The pants have lots of pockets. The woman doesn't know why she's seeing this in her head. Then she pushes the image from her mind.

Officer Surdam is driving his Dodge Charger Police Interceptor back to the station. He likes his new car, with its powerful HEMI engine and it's bright LED lights. He's driving along slow, and it's good too, because if he was going any faster he would have hit the woman that ran out in front of him. He slams on the brakes and beeps the horn before stepping out of the car. The woman looks at him and turns away, but then stops and looks back. "You alright?" The woman doesn't respond. She just looks at him. He notices something about the way she's looking at him, it's odd. There's something in her eyes. Fear. Distrust. She's pretty, Surdam thinks to himself.

The woman is still resisting the urge to look behind her, and pushes forward towards the street. She's tired. Too tired to be running like this, this fast. She'll stop in front of the bank on the other side of the street, where there's a streetlight. She'll call a cab, take that home. She runs out into the street and hears screeching tires and a loud car horn. She stops, then reminds herself of what she was just running from. She can make out the words "Police" in big letters on the side. She stops, thinking maybe she can trust this person. She flashes back to what her dad told her when she was 14, only two days before he died: "Never trust anyone." She turns and gets ready to run, then looks back at the officer. He asks if she's alright. Of course she isn't, she was just chased by someone who probably wanted to rape her. She doesn't respond. She's not looking at him anymore anyway, she's looking at the grey car that just turned onto the street behind him.

"Ma'am, are you alright?" Officer Surdam asks again, removing his flashlight and shining it at her. She flinches away from the bright light. Well, she's responsive, at least. He hears a car behind him and instinctively turns to look. Just a grey car driving down the road. There's a man in the driver's seat, and he's holding something. He's holding a gun, an assault rifle. He's pointing it at the officer, his hands aren't on the wheel. He's smiling, and looking straight at Surdam, never looking at the road. The look strikes fear into the officer's eyes before he remembers that this isn't real. It's not real, it's not real, it's not real... He keeps telling himself this, closes his eyes for a moment, before he opens them again. The man in the car has stopped, probably because the police car is blocking the road, but he's not holding a gun. He never was. Iraq took a toll on Officer Surdam. He shakes his head and turns back around. "Ma'am, please step over to the side of the road, I need to move my vehicle." The woman starts to move towards the sidewalk as Officer Surdam parks his vehicle in the parking place on the side of the road. The woman still is looking past him it seems, but Officer Surdam doesn't really care. He just wants to make sure she's alright and then go home and drown his PTSD in whiskey.

The officer turns around to look at the car. He stands there for a moment like a deer in headlights before closing his eyes tightly. He opens them again and shakes his head. He asks her to move to the sidewalk. Great, now she's going to be stuck here for awhile. He moves his car and steps back out, shining his flashlight at her again.

Surdam shines the flashlight at her and asks her again: "Ma'am, are you alright?" More stern this time. Maybe that was too stern. The woman finally opens her mouth. "Yes... yes I'm fine. I just want to go home. Please." She has a British accent. Hot.

"Ma'am, have you been drinking tonight?"

"No, I haven't been drinking, I was just out for a jog. What do you want?"

"I just want to go home, please."

He looks at her suspiciously. She's hiding something.

"Ma'am, do you have anything illegal on your person? Narcotics, alcohol, weapons...?"

"No, no I don't."

He pauses. "Is there something you want to tell me?"

She can't tell him about the man in the car, can she? He still hasn't moved. He's sitting in the street, waiting. Waiting for her. "Er... I..." She whispers, "Not here."

Now he's intrigued. "Does it have anything to do with the grey car behind me?" He asks, matching her quiet tone. She leans in to answer, and as she does she notices something, something that make her heart stop.

He's wearing an odd grey dress shirt with a badge etc. on it. But his pants aren't standard issue police officer pants. She knows what those look like, her fathers' closet was full of them. But he's not wearing them; he's wearing black tactical pants with kneepads.
